facts.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/layout_result.h (lines 41-65; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file)
facts.evidence: enum EStatus { kSuccess = 0, kBfcBlockOffsetResolved = 1, kNeedsEarlierBreak = 2, kOutOfFragmentainerSpace = 3, kNeedsLineClampRelayout = 4, kDisableFragmentation = 5,

facts.claim: Layout algorithms are template specializations required to implement ComputeMinMaxSizes() and Layout(); the layout/build.gni lists 28 *_layout_algorithm.h files (block, column, flex, grid, grid_lanes, inline, table×3, mathml×9, page/print×3, ...).
facts.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/layout_algorithm.h (lines 43-56; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file) and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/build.gni (lines whole file; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file)
facts.evidence: Subclassed template specializations (actual layout algorithms) are required to define the following two functions: MinMaxSizesResult ComputeMinMaxSizes(const MinMaxSizesInput&); const LayoutResult* Layout();

facts.claim: Layout results are cached on the LayoutBox and reused when the constraint space is identical and the node is not marked for layout; separate measure results are kept for the measure pass.
facts.source: src/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/layout_ng.md:75-95 and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/layout_box.h (lines 485-515; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file)
facts.evidence: Returns the last layout result for this block flow with the given constraint space and break token, or null if it is not up-to-date or otherwise unavailable.

facts.claim: The immutable fragment tree forbids parent pointers and downward data bubbling so that unchanged subtrees can be reused and only the 'spine' rebuilt on incremental layout.
facts.evidence: We don't allow any 'up' references in the tree. (A child can't have a pointer to its parent.) ... typically we only need to rebuild the spine of the tree.

facts.claim: LayoutNG's explicit input/output structures with measure and layout caches return flex/grid layout from exponential to O(n); the grid case was fixed in Chrome 93.
facts.evidence: we have built caches of the measure and layout passes. This brings the complexity back to O(n), resulting in predictably linear performance. ... This is fixed in Chrome 93 as a result of moving Grid onto the new architecture

facts.claim: Block layout lets children place themselves in the BFC via an optional LayoutResult::BfcOffset; unpositioned floats and margin collapsing are resolved by aborting and re-running layout once a BFC offset is known.
facts.evidence: Once something resolves its BfcOffset ... we abort the layout telling the ancestor chain about the new BFCOffset, and restart layout. Inside this second pass, all unpositioned floats now position themselves immediately

facts.claim: Margin collapsing follows max(pos_margins) + min(neg_margins), implemented with a MarginStrut that is threaded through layout as input plus an end strut as output.
facts.evidence: The rule here is: max(pos_margins) + min(neg_margins). ... We invert the problem. A fragment now only produces an _end_ margin strut. The _start_ margin strut becomes an input

facts.claim: Once positioned, floats live in an append-only ExclusionSpace that answers layout-opportunity, clearance and last-float-offset queries.
facts.evidence: Once a float is positioned, everything else float related is handled by the ExclusionSpace. Mutating the exclusion space only happens by adding additional exclusions.

facts.claim: Inline layout runs four phases — pre-layout (InlineItem list), line breaking (InlineItemResult), line-box construction (LogicalLineItem), fragment generation (FragmentItem) — with text shaped by HarfBuzz and bidi resolved by ICU.
facts.evidence: ShapeText: Shapes the segments using HarfBuzz. ... The core logic is implemented in BidiParagraph, which is a thin wrapper for ICU BiDi.

facts.claim: FragmentItem represents a text run or box in an inline formatting context in a flat list (FragmentItems) that uses less memory than full fragments; the data-structures article says each entry is (object, number of descendants) in DFS order.
facts.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/layout/inline/fragment_item.h (lines 57-61; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file) and https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/renderingng-data-structures
facts.evidence: This class consumes less memory than a full fragment, and can be stored in a flat list (FragmentItems) for easier and faster traversal.

facts.claim: 'Culled inline' skips box fragments for inline boxes that affect neither layout nor paint (e.g. <b> around text) — ShouldCreateBoxFragment() is computed at style recalc and never reset once set.
facts.evidence: This optimization is called "culled inline" in the code. ... To mitigate multiple layouts by like hover highlighting, ShouldCreateBoxFragment() will not be reset once it's set.

facts.claim: Block fragmentation attaches BlockBreakTokens (a tree, including break-before tokens) to fragments; the next fragmentainer resumes from them, and column boxes are themselves fragmentainer fragments produced by BlockLayoutAlgorithm under ColumnLayoutAlgorithm.
facts.evidence: When we break before or inside a node, we attach a break token to the resulting fragment. The break tokens form a tree structure for each parent we need to break and resume inside of

facts.claim: Painting and hit-testing traverse the physical fragment tree, not the LayoutObject tree, which is what makes multicol and other fragmentation natural in NG.
facts.evidence: We'll paint and hit-test by traversing the physical fragment tree, rather than traversing the LayoutObject tree. This is important for block fragmentation

facts.claim: LayoutNG milestones: first release in Chrome 77 (2019), covering "regular block container layout, inline layout, floats and out-of-flow positioning"; core block fragmentation in Chrome 102, flex/grid fragmentation in 103, table fragmentation in 106, printing in 108, after which "the legacy engine is no longer used to perform layout". The same article immediately qualifies that sentence: "we do rely on some legacy data structures for JavaScript APIs that read layout information, such as offsetLeft and offsetTop" — legacy *layout* ended at 108, legacy data structures did not. Chrome 108 reached stable on 2022-11-29, so the RenderingNG overview's 2021 row ("Ship everything else.") was a roadmap that overran by about a year.
facts.evidence: Core fragmentation ... shipped in Chrome 102. Flex and grid fragmentation shipped in Chrome 103, and table fragmentation shipped in Chrome 106. Lastly, printing shipped in Chrome 108. ... As of Chrome 108, the legacy engine is no longer used to perform layout.

facts.claim: core/paint converts the LayoutObject tree into cc::Layers with display item lists and cc::PropertyTrees, in two lifecycle phases: PrePaint (invalidation + property trees) and Paint (display list → chunks → commit to compositor).
facts.evidence: PrePaint (kInPrePaint): Paint invalidation ... Builds paint property trees. Paint (kInPaint): Walks the LayoutObject tree and creates a display item list. Groups the display list into paint chunks which share the same property tree state.

facts.claim: PrePaintTreeWalk walks the whole layout tree from the root LocalFrameView across frame boundaries in pre-order, which is what makes parent-containing-block computation cheap.
facts.evidence: This is an in-order tree traversal which is important for efficiently computing DOM-order hierarchy such as the parent containing block.

facts.claim: Blink has four paint property trees — transform, clip, effect, scroll — with parent pointers only; each paint chunk carries one node of each.
facts.evidence: Paint properties are represented by four paint property trees (transform, clip, effect and scroll) each of which contains corresponding type of paint property nodes. Each paint property node has a pointer to the parent node.

facts.claim: A transform node holds a 4x4 matrix, 3D origin, a flatten-to-parent flag and a rendering-context id; scroll offsets are stored as 2D transforms so geometry math only deals with transforms.
facts.evidence: To ensure geometry operations are simple and only deal with transforms, the scroll offset is stored as a 2d transform in the transform tree.

facts.claim: ObjectPaintProperties enumerates 42 node slots per fragment (NodeId::kNumFields = kClipAlias + 1): 15 transforms plus alias, 1 scroll, 11 effects plus alias, 12 clips plus alias.
facts.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/paint/object_paint_properties.h (lines 116-176; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file)
facts.evidence: kPaintOffsetTranslation = kFirstTransform, kStickyTranslation = 1, kAnchorPositionScrollTranslation = 2, kElementCanvasTransform = 3, ... kLineClampFloatClip = 40, kLastClip = kLineClampFloatClip, kClipAlias = 41, kNumFields = kClipAlias + 1

facts.claim: An element's transform subtree is ordered PaintOffsetTranslation → StickyTranslation → AnchorPositionScrollTranslation → ElementCanvasTransform → Translate → Rotate → Scale → Offset → Transform → ContentTranslation → Perspective → ReplacedContentTransform | ScrollTranslation.
facts.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/paint/object_paint_properties.h (lines 184-256; GitHub mirror of main, fetched 2026-09-18; local sparse checkout omits this file)
facts.evidence: [ PaintOffsetTranslation ] Normally paint offset is accumulated without creating a node until we see, for example, transform or position:fixed.

facts.claim: Three dirty bits — NeedsPaintPropertyUpdate, SubtreeNeedsPaintPropertyUpdate, DescendantNeedsPaintPropertyUpdate — bound the pre-paint walk, and contain:paint isolation nodes (alias nodes) stop forced subtree walks.
facts.evidence: the isolation boundary is achieved using alias nodes, which are nodes that are put in place on an isolated element for clip, transform, and effect trees.

facts.claim: Without multicol there is one FragmentData per LayoutObject; with N columns each fragment gets its own property nodes, and the child's i-th fragment parents to the parent's i-th fragment.
facts.evidence: if there are 3 columns and both a parent and child LayoutObject have a transform, there will be 3 FragmentData objects for the parent, 3 for the child, each FragmentData will have its own TransformPaintPropertyNode

facts.claim: Simple transform and opacity style changes bypass the property-tree builder via a pending direct-update list executed in PrePaintTreeWalk::WalkTree.
facts.evidence: Current updates that are checked for an optimized update are transform updates and opacity updates.

facts.claim: Within a PaintLayer, paint walks the PhysicalFragment tree in paint order via static painters (e.g. BoxFragmentPainter) into a single PaintController per LocalFrameView, which segments display items into PaintChunks sharing a property tree state.

facts.claim: The CompositeAfterPaint launch plan (Philip Rogers, paint-dev, 26 May - 4 June 2021) did open with "Jul 25: Enable by default at tip-of-tree M94" followed by "Sep 19: 99% finch trial in M93 Stable", but Rogers withdrew that ordering inside the same thread after pushback from Xianzhu Wang and Stephen Chenney: "Pipelining the feature in two releases (finch M93, stable M94) is too aggressive". The agreed final schedule was a 1% Finch trial in M93+ stable from 20 Aug, ramp from 14 Sep, and "Oct 6: Enable at TOT in M96". The tip-of-tree flip actually landed on 2021-10-27 (commit 1479240c28d2, main@{#935633}, flipping CompositeAfterPaint from status "test" to "stable" in runtime_enabled_features.json5) — after the M96 branch point, i.e. at tip-of-tree for M97. M94 is the Finch-launch milestone, not the tip-of-tree-default milestone.

facts.claim: cc has two raster modes — software raster in worker threads and GPU raster over the command buffer — chosen from RasterContextProvider capabilities; switching modes destroys all resources.

facts.claim: Three RasterBufferProviders exist: ZeroCopy (shared memory / GpuMemoryBuffer), OneCopy (software bitmap uploaded in the GPU process), Gpu (paint commands over the command buffer); GPU raster is serialized to one worker thread by a lock.

facts.claim: Oilpan is the garbage collector for Blink objects; the Blink doc defers the general design to the cppgc README in V8 and documents only Blink-specific extensions.
facts.evidence: Oilpan is a garbage collector (GC) for Blink objects. ... The general design of Oilpan is explained in the [Oilpan README](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8/+/main/include/cppgc/README.md). This section focuses on the Blink specific extensions to that design.

facts.claim: Oilpan heaps are per-thread and never shared; threads must attach via ThreadState::AttachMainThread() or AttachCurrentThread(); an object belongs to the thread that allocated it.
facts.evidence: Oilpan assumes heaps are not shared among threads. Threads that want to allocate Oilpan objects must be *attached* to Oilpan, by calling either `blink::ThreadState::AttachMainThread()` or `blink::ThreadState::AttachCurrentThread()`. ... An object belongs to the thread it is allocated on.

facts.claim: Blink partitions the Oilpan heap: collection backings go to compactable custom spaces; Node, CSSValue and LayoutObject go to typed custom spaces.
facts.evidence: Objects that are a collection backing are allocated in one of the collection backing *compactable* custom spaces. Objects that are a Node, a CSSValue or a LayoutObject are allocated in one of the typed custom spaces.

facts.claim: Blink runs concurrent marking and sweeping (except at thread termination/heap destruction), schedules precise GCs from the message loop, and falls back to conservative GC on allocation under memory pressure.
facts.evidence: Blink uses concurrent garbage collection (marking and sweeping), except for during thread termination and heap destruction. Blink tries to schedule GCs through the message loop where it is known that no objects are referred to from the native stack. When under memory pressure, Blink triggers a conservative GC on allocations.

facts.claim: GC-managed classes inherit GarbageCollected<T>, are created via MakeGarbageCollected<T>, cannot use operator new, and must never be deleted manually.
facts.evidence: Instances of such classes are said to be *on Oilpan heap* ... Instances of a garbage-collected class can be created/allocated through `MakeGarbageCollected<T>`. Declaring a class as garbage collected disallows the use of `operator new`. It is not allowed to free garbage-collected object with `delete`

facts.claim: Non-trivially-destructible GC classes are finalized automatically at an arbitrary later time; destructors must not touch other on-heap objects because finalization order is undefined.
facts.evidence: Non-trivially destructible classes will be automatically finalized. ... Note that finalization is done at an arbitrary time after the object becomes unreachable. Any destructor executed within the finalization period *must not* touch any other on-heap object because destructors can be executed in any order.

facts.claim: The 'leftmost derivation rule': GarbageCollected<T> (or a class deriving from it) must be the first base so every on-heap object has one canonical address; other bases holding Members must be GarbageCollectedMixin.
facts.evidence: `GarbageCollected<T>` or any class deriving from `GarbageCollected<T>`, directly or indirectly, must be the first element in its base class list (called "leftmost derivation rule"). This rule is needed to assure each on-heap object has its own canonical address.

facts.claim: A pre-finalizer (USING_PRE_FINALIZER) runs before sweeping starts and may touch other on-heap objects, unlike a destructor; pre-finalizers cost a scan of all registered pre-finalizers at every GC.
facts.evidence: It is invoked before the sweeping phase starts to allow a pre-finalizer to touch any other on-heap objects which is forbidden from destructors. ... the garbage-collector needs to iterate all registered pre-finalizers at every GC. Therefore, a pre-finalizer should be avoided unless it is really necessary.

facts.claim: DISALLOW_NEW classes can live on stack, embedded, or as collection values but need a Trace() called by the embedder; STACK_ALLOCATED classes may hold raw pointers to GC objects and need no Trace() because conservative scanning finds them.
facts.evidence: Classes with this annotation do not need to define a `Trace()` method as they are on the stack, and are automatically traced and kept alive should a conservative GC be required. ... Marking a class as STACK_ALLOCATED implicitly implies DISALLOW_NEW

facts.claim: Raw pointers to on-heap objects are forbidden except on the stack (locals, parameters, return values), which is the only legal use.
facts.evidence: Using raw pointers to garbage-collected objects on-heap is forbidden and will yield in memory corruptions. On-stack references to garbage-collected object (including function parameters and return types), on the other hand, must use raw pointers.

facts.claim: Member<T> is a strong traced reference allowed to form cycles (unlike scoped_refptr); WeakMember<T> is cleared to nullptr during GC, with some latency, and has GC overhead so should be used only when the owner can outlive the pointee.
facts.evidence: Unlike `scoped_refptr<T>`, it is okay to form a reference cycle with members ... The pointer in a `WeakMember<T>` can become `nullptr` when the object gets garbage-collected. ... The use of `WeakMember<T>` incurs some overhead in garbage collector's performance. Use it sparingly.

facts.claim: UntracedMember<T> is ignored by Oilpan (neither keeps alive nor is cleared) and is meant only for custom weakness implementations.
facts.evidence: `UntracedMember<T>` represents a reference to a garbage collected object which is ignored by Oilpan. ... Users should avoid using `UntracedMember<T>` in any case other than when implementing custom weakness semantics.

facts.claim: Persistent<T> roots an object from off-heap code; persistents maintain a global list (overhead), and a cycle through Persistent/Member/RefPtr/OwnPtr leaks all objects in it.
facts.evidence: Persistents have a small unavoidable overhead because they require maintaining a list of all persistents. ... If a reference cycle is formed with `Persistent`s, `Member`s, `RefPtr`s and `OwnPtr`s, all the objects in the cycle **will leak**

facts.claim: CrossThreadPersistent may point into another thread's heap but signals poor design; CrossThreadHandle/CrossThreadWeakHandle only allow thread-safe copy/move/destroy and deref on the owning thread, for delegating work to other threads.
facts.evidence: In general, Blink does not support shared-memory concurrency designs. The need of cross-thread persistents may indicate a poor design ... The difference to `CrossThreadPersistent<T>` is that these handles prohibit deref on any thread except the thread that owns the object pointed to.

facts.claim: A Trace(Visitor*) const method must visitor->Trace every Member/WeakMember/DISALLOW_NEW field and delegate to each GC base; it should avoid branches/loops that depend on non-const fields because that races with concurrent marking.
facts.evidence: Generally, a `Trace()` method would be just a sequence of delegations ... In case a branch is unavoidable, the branch condition should depend only on const fields of the object. ... Using non-const fields in `Trace()` methods may cause data races and other issues in the GC.

facts.claim: Heap collections mirror WTF/stdlib containers: HeapVector, HeapDeque, HeapHashMap, HeapHashSet, HeapLinkedHashSet, HeapHashCountedSet; they must be traced, may be inlined in objects and used on stack, and must not hold Persistent types.
facts.evidence: | std::vector | blink::Vector | blink::HeapVector | ... Heap collections are regular heap objects and thus must be properly traced from a `Trace` method. They can also be inlined into other objects for performance reasons and are allowed to be directly used on stack.

facts.claim: Weak collections distinguish pure weakness (all entries WeakMember: entries removed when any dies) from mixed weakness in HeapHashMap (ephemeron semantics); WeakMember is not supported in HeapVector/HeapDeque; iterators strongify the collection.
facts.evidence: Pure weakness: Oilpan will automatically remove the entries from the container if any of its declared `WeakMember<T>` fields points to a dead object. Mixed weakness: Oilpan applies ephemeron semantics ... Weak references (e.g. `WeakMember<T>`) are not supported in sequential containers such as `HeapVector` or `HeapDeque`.

facts.claim: Custom weak callbacks are registered from Trace() via RegisterWeakCallback/RegisterWeakCallbackMethod and only run if the registering object survived; fields under custom weakness must be UntracedMember.
facts.evidence: `RegisterWeakCallback`: Used to add custom weak callbacks of the form `void(void*, const blink::LivenessBroker&)`. ... the custom weakness callback in this example is only executed if `W` is alive and properly traced. If `W` itself dies than the callback will not be executed.

facts.claim: CIPD versions are one of: an instance ID (content hash), a unique key:value tag such as git_revision:deadbeef, or a ref such as latest, which chrome-infra builders move to every new upload; platform-specific packages end in /<os>-<arch>.
facts.evidence: A package instance can be marked with tags, where a tag is a colon-separated key-value pair, e.g. `"git_revision:deadbeef"`. If some tag points to only one instance, such tag can be used as version identifier. ... chrome-infra continuous builders always update the `"latest"` ref of a package to the instance that they upload.

facts.claim: An instance ID is the hex SHA1 for legacy instances (40 chars) and otherwise base64url-without-padding of the digest followed by one hash-algo byte — so the DEPS values like 'TX7HeY1_1JLwFVx-xiETOpT8YK4W5CbyO26SpmaMA0IC' are 44-char SHA-256 IDs; the gn instance 2529a6e6… encodes to 'JSmm5hi-E9BbdhobW14vDIvT5cWS0Mi_Fq_tErYxTxIB'.
facts.evidence: // Its exact form depends on a hash being used: // - SHA1: Instance IDs are hex encoded SHA1 digests, in lowercase. // - Everything else: base64(digest + []byte{ref.HashAlgo}), where base64 is without padding and using URL-safe charset.

facts.claim: The migration was announced on chromium-dev by Josip Sokcevic on 2 March 2023 under the subject 'Moving chromium/src git dependencies to git submodules'.
facts.evidence: We are moving away from git dependencies being managed by gclient DEPS to native Git submodules. You can review our plans and reasoning in this document

facts.claim: The announced motivation is simpler tooling and, long term, obtaining Chromium with a plain git client.
facts.evidence: We are doing this to simplify tooling used by Chromium and unlock our long term vision of using industry standard systems and getting the Chromium codebase with just git client (i.e. via git clone).

facts.claim: Stage 1 (ETA 2023 Q2) added .gitmodules and gitlinks alongside DEPS with no UI change.
facts.evidence: In the first stage, we will introduce git submodules (.gitmodules and gitlinks) alongside DEPS. As part of this effort, we will be restructuring our DEPS to be submodule compatible. ... ETA: 2023 Q2.

facts.claim: Stage 2 (ETA 2023 Q4) was defined as making submodules the source of truth and dropping git deps from DEPS, with at least three months' notice for DEPS-parsing tools.
facts.evidence: In the second stage, we will be using git submodules as source of truth and git dependencies will be dropped from DEPS files. We understand that some tools parse DEPS files directly so we will give sufficient time for this migration to happen (at least three months). ... ETA: 2023 Q4

facts.claim: Stage 3 (unscheduled) is the only stage in which git itself would manage submodules and the UI would change.
facts.evidence: In the last stage, we will start using the git submodule command to manage git submodules. ... you can expect some UI changes since git will start tracking submodules. ETA: unscheduled.

facts.claim: The linked design doc is 'Chromium Browser development using Git submodules', by sokcevic@chromium.org, dated 8 Feb 2023, status Published, and is fetchable as plain text via /export?format=txt.
facts.evidence: Chromium Browser development using Git submodules / Author: sokcevic@chromium.org / Date: Feb 8, 2023 / Status: Published

facts.claim: The design doc's objective names the concrete tooling win: no more synthetic commit for the codesearch/chromium/src repo.
facts.evidence: It will simplify tooling used by Chromium, e.g. we will no longer need a synthetic commit for codesearch/chromium/src resulting in showing real time history in Code Search.

facts.claim: The design doc frames the change as adopting a standard system so that submodule-aware tools need no Chromium special-casing.
facts.evidence: By moving to a more standard dependency system we can take advantage of tools, both existing and planned, that understand git submodules without needing special casing for Chromium and DEPS.

facts.claim: The long-term vision in the design doc is a git-clone-able Chromium.
facts.evidence: Our long term vision is to be able to use git clone to fetch the chromium codebase and chromium related projects and this is one of the steps to get us there.

facts.claim: Design-doc milestone 2 ('Gclient uses git submodules information as source of truth') is tracked by crbug.com/1409734 with ETA 2023 Q4 and explicitly excludes git submodule operations.
facts.evidence: Remove git dependencies from DEPS. gclient will rely on information from git submodules (.gitmodules file and gitlinks), but it won't use any git submodule operations. ... Tracking bug: https://crbug.com/1409734 ETA: 2023 Q4.

facts.claim: Design-doc milestone 3 ('Git client manages git submodules', crbug.com/1417344) is labelled aspirational and requires changes to git itself.
facts.evidence: Remove custom cloning of git repositories and rely on `git submodule` porcelain. ... This is an aspirational goal, it will require changes to the git client. ... Tracking bug: https://crbug.com/1417344 ETA: unknown

facts.claim: CIPD dependencies were never planned to move out of DEPS.
facts.evidence: Yes, we have no plans for CIPD dependencies so they will remain in DEPS.

facts.claim: gclient, not git, manages submodules for stages 1 and 2; stage 3 waits on comfort with the git CLI.
facts.evidence: That's why we will still rely on depot_tools/gclient to manage git submodules for the first two stages. We will move onto the third stage (Git client manages git submodules) only when we are comfortable with the Git CLI

facts.claim: Git-native filtering of unwanted submodules (git attributes) was tried and rejected on UX grounds, and is a precondition for stage 3.
facts.evidence: We experimented with git attributes to be able to filter out repositories that we don't want, but the UX wasn't great. ... However, this will need to be solved before we start the last stage of the migration.

facts.claim: Submodules were planned only for repos whose DEPS Chromium recurses into (recursedeps), which explains why V8/Skia/WebRTC/PDFium never needed them.
facts.evidence: The plan is to add git submodules to all repositories where we parse their DEPS file (ie all recursedeps entries)

facts.claim: Absolute submodule URLs are unavoidable because Chromium depends on about a dozen googlesource hosts (the 2026 .gitmodules uses 11 distinct hosts).
facts.evidence: We already rely on about a dozen other hosts

facts.claim: ANGLE raised that AOSP forbids submodules, so ANGLE's AOSP roll script must strip .gitmodules.

facts.claim: Ken Russell noted in March 2023 that conditional submodules were undefined by the design doc and bugs; the June 2023 depot_tools doc answered this with the gclient-condition key.

facts.claim: The mechanism doc is 'depot_tools submodules support' by aravindvasudev@chromium.org, dated 20 Jun 2023, and it declares replacing DEPS a non-goal.
facts.evidence: Non-goals (Optional) 1. Replacing DEPS with the git submodules completely. The major goal here is to use git submodules where possible and not to replace the DEPS file.

facts.claim: The depot_tools doc lists the breaking changes of SUBMODULES mode: no branch/HEAD pins, no variable-based overrides, and no git deps in DEPS.
facts.evidence: Breaking changes 1. No longer possible to point a git dependency to non-commit (e.g. branch or HEAD). 2. No longer possible to override hosts, repo, or commit hash using DEPS variables. 3. (indirect) DEPS file no longer contains git dependencies.

facts.claim: recursedeps cannot move to .gitmodules because git has no selective recursion; CIPD and hooks also stay in DEPS.
facts.evidence: the script will still rely heavily on the DEPS file for all the other information such as the CIPD dependencies and the hooks. Selective recursion is not natively supported by git submodules and hence recursedeps will stay within DEPS.

facts.claim: After migration to SUBMODULES, parent repos and .gclient files lose the ability to override a child's git deps via variables.
facts.evidence: parent repositories will no longer be able to override dependencies using gclient variables after migrating from DEPS to submodules, nor users will be able to override variables via their .gclient files

facts.claim: Conditions are stored as a custom gclient-condition key in .gitmodules that native git ignores (so plain git would check out every dep).
facts.evidence: Even though the native git submodules may never read this condition (and thus always checkout all deps), gclient can be updated to read/write this attribute (allowing gclient users to not checkout all deps)

facts.claim: The three git_dependencies states are defined as DEPS (default), SYNC (intermediate) and SUBMODULES (submodules only).
facts.evidence: DEPS -> Only use DEPS file for read/write (default). SYNC -> Keep DEPS and submodules in sync for write; assume they are in-sync for read. Useful intermediate state for migration. SUBMODULES -> Use only git submodules for read/write.

facts.claim: The depot_tools doc restated the 2023 Q4 target for gclient relying entirely on submodules.
facts.evidence: gclient completely relying on git submodules for its git dependencies will be completed by 2023 Q4. The user interface will remain the same after the migration.

facts.claim: The .git URL suffix was stripped from .gitmodules in Nov 2023 because submodule-consuming systems handle it badly, while DEPS kept it because other tools expect it - a small example of DEPS-parsers constraining the migration.

facts.claim: gclient gitmodules started writing gclient-recursedeps into .gitmodules in Oct 2024, with no presubmit enforcing it.

facts.claim: Goma was a distributed compiler service for open-source projects such as Chromium and Android, positioned as a replacement for distcc+ccache.

facts.claim: Goma's basic model: hook a compile request, send it to backend compile servers so builds can run at very high -j, and cache compile results on the backend.
facts.evidence: Goma hooks a compile request, and sends it to a backend compile server. If you have plenty of backend servers, a lot of compile can be processed in parallel, for example, -j100, -j500 or -j1000. Also, the Goma backend caches the compile result.

facts.evidence: distcc needs a cluster configuration and a cluster of machines. goma on the other hand runs sandboxed compiler binaries in google's datacenters, where thousands of machines are available.

facts.claim: Siso's runRemote algorithm: run the first startLocal steps locally; check the remote cache using the deps log; run locally if local resources are idle (fast local); otherwise execute remotely with deps-log inputs, retry with a full deps scan, and finally fall back to local — each fallback type is counted and the build fails on TooManyFallbackError.
facts.evidence: 1. for initial steps of startLocal, run locally. 2. Check remote cache with deps log if available. 3. If local resource is idle, run locally. 4. Otherwise, try running a remote execution with deps log. 5. If it failed, it will retry a remote execution with deps scan. 6. If it still failed, it will fallback to local execution.

facts.claim: The bootstrap library explains the purpose: property changes are versioned with the source, applied during CQ runs, and a builder building an old revision gets the properties set at that revision; the bootstrapper is a passthrough luciexe.
facts.evidence: Enabling bootstrapping for a builder provides versioning of the properties: property changes for CQ builders will be applied during the CQ run and when building a revision of code, the properties that are applied will be the properties that were set for the builder at that revision. This is accomplished by the use of a passthrough-style bootstrapper luciexe.

facts.claim: lucicfg package dependency resolution is a Minimal-Version-Selection variant: a dependency may be imported at the requested or a newer revision on the same ref, never older, so library APIs must stay backward compatible.

It means the public API of imported packages should generally be backward compatible.

facts.claim: docs/infra/builder_types.md (Q2 2025) says nearly 100% of Chromium infra workloads are Swarming tasks and nearly every Buildbucket build is backed by a Swarming task; it catalogues four patterns: all-in-one with local tests, all-in-one with swarmed tests, parent-child (builder-tester) split, and orchestrator-compilator.
facts.evidence: As of writing (Q2 2025), nearly 100% of all workloads in Chromium's infra run as Swarming tasks. ... Consequently, it's not inaccurate to conceptualize a Buildbucket build simply as a Swarming task whose command is its "recipe".

facts.claim: builder_types.md: in the builder-tester split the compile runs on an over-provisioned (32/64-core) parent that immediately picks up new work, while the child tester runs on 2-4 core machines and may discard piled-up triggers; e.g. Mac Builder feeds Mac13 Tests and mac14-tests.
facts.evidence: Importantly, the first build does not wait around for the second after triggering... If the situation arises where the first builder is cycling faster than the second and piling on build triggers, the child builder will often take only the most recent trigger, and discard the rest.

facts.claim: builder_types.md: the orchestrator-compilator split keeps one user-facing build (the orchestrator) that immediately triggers a compilator; the compilator compiles, isolates and runs checkout-needing tests, then hands binaries to the orchestrator, which runs on 2- or 4-core machines.
facts.evidence: In this model, a single builder called the "orchestrator" runs for the entire duration and is the sole/primary user-facing build. However, upon running it immediately triggers a second builder called the "compilator". This compilator builder handles all compilation while the original orchestrator is simply sleeping.

facts.claim: docs/infra/cq.md: the CQ runs what commit-queue.cfg specifies; a CQ build compiles and runs affected suites '(with patch)', retries failed shards identically '(retry shards with patch)', then reruns failures '(without patch)' and only fails if a test failed with patch but passed without.

Rerun each failing test suite in isolation... * Fail the build if there are tests which failed in both '(with patch)' and '(retry shards with patch)' but passed in '(without patch)'. facts.claim: The polymorphic launcher pattern lets one launcher builder act for many target builders: chromium-luci's polymorphic.star defaults the executable to recipe:chromium_polymorphic/launcher and injects runner_builder / target_builders (with builder_id, optional dimensions and tester_filter) into the launcher's properties at lucicfg generation time.
facts.evidence: The launcher enables creating a single polymorphic builder that can be launched to perform operations on behalf of 1 or more target builders. This prevents needing to create and maintain the configuration for builders to mimic the standard builders

facts.claim: The CV tryjob verifier documents that tryjob results older than one day are ignored; the 24 h reuse window is the documented default.
facts.evidence: CQ automatically retries failed tryjobs and only allows CL to land if each builder has succeeded in the latest retry. If a given tryjob result is too old (>1 day) it is ignored.

facts.claim: disable_reuse forces a fresh build per CQ attempt; by default CV may reuse a successful build triggered before the attempt started, typically disabled for presubmit builders.
facts.evidence: Optional. If true, a fresh build will be required for each CQ attempt. Default is false, meaning CQ may re-use a successful build triggered before current CQ attempt started.

facts.claim: disable_reuse_footers disables reuse when a listed footer is added, removed or changes value; keys must be normalized dash-case.

facts.claim: cancel_stale (default YES) cancels running or not-yet-started CQ builds when a 'substantially different' patchset is uploaded; CV snapshots the value at Run creation.

facts.claim: reuse_window switches reuse from elapsed time to commit distance; it requires monotonic Cr-Commit-Position footers (git-numberer) and is allowlisted (Chromium/Chrome); unset means the 24 h time window.
facts.evidence: This allows reusing past successful builds based on "commit distance" (number of commits between the build's base revision and the branch tip) rather than just elapsed time. ... If unset, default 24h time-based reuse window is used.

facts.claim: ReuseWindow has a single field, max_commit_distance (uint32 > 0): a build is not reusable if tip position minus its base position exceeds it.
facts.evidence: If the distance between the commit position of the base revision of a previous build and the current branch tip exceeds this value, the build cannot be reused. ... uint32 max_commit_distance = 1 [(validate.rules).uint32.gt = 0];

facts.claim: Reusability is a three-valued decision: PENDING/TRIGGERED-and-fresh builds 'may' be reused, ENDED+SUCCEEDED+fresh+mode-allowed builds are reused, and ENDED-failed, CANCELLED or UNTRIGGERED builds are denied.
facts.evidence: Tryjob *can* be reused iff the Tryjob ends successfully and is fresh enough against target requirement def (i.e created within `staleTryjobAge` or within the commit distance limit). Tryjob *may* be reused if the Tryjob is fresh enough and still running or hasn't started yet.

facts.claim: With max_commit_distance set, CV compares the build's OutputGitilesCommit position with the branch tip and falls back to the time window on any error (missing metadata, Gitiles failure, tip behind build).

facts.claim: The branch tip position is resolved by a Gitiles Log(PageSize 1) call parsing the tip's Cr-Commit-Position footer, cached 15 s with a 5 s timeout; a ref mismatch (new branch whose tip still carries main's footer) safely falls back to the time window.
facts.evidence: Note that when a new branch is branched off main, its tip commit initially retains main's Cr-Commit-Position footer. This ref mismatch causes resolveBranchTip to return an error, safely falling back to the time-based window until the first new commit lands on the branch.

facts.claim: EquivalentPatchsetRange walks Gerrit revision kinds newest-first: NO_CHANGE, NO_CODE_CHANGE, MERGE_FIRST_PARENT_UPDATE, TRIVIAL_REBASE and TRIVIAL_REBASE_WITH_MESSAGE_UPDATE extend the equivalence range; REWORK stops it. So a trivial rebase keeps the reuse key.
facts.evidence: Gerrit categorises each new patchset (aka Revision) according to difference from prior one. The rebases are counted as equivalent, even though dependencies may have changed. Thus, only REWORK changes code.

facts.claim: Gerrit defines TRIVIAL_REBASE as a new patchset with the same commit message and the same diff including context lines, i.e. a conflict-free rebase or no parent change at all.

facts.claim: Autosharder formula: optimal = ceil(current_shards * (runtime - overhead) / (target_runtime - overhead)), using the 80th-percentile shard runtime over a 14-day BigQuery window with >=1500 non-experimental samples. The ceil is floored at 1 (`integer_optimal_shard_count = max(math.ceil(optimal_shard_count), 1)`). The defaults DEFAULT_OVERHEAD_MIN = 1.0 min and ANDROID_OVERHEAD_MIN = 2.0 min apply only when no measured overhead was stored; the [MIN_OVERHEAD_MIN 0.2, MAX_OVERHEAD_MIN 4.0] clamp is applied by the overhead setter to the BigQuery-measured per-suite overhead (p50 task setup + p50 test-harness overhead, converted to minutes), not to the defaults.
facts.evidence: autosharder.py:148-160: "optimal_shard_count = (self.shard_count * (self.runtime - self.overhead)) / (target_runtime - self.overhead) ... integer_optimal_shard_count = max(math.ceil(optimal_shard_count), 1)"; :96-110: "MIN_SAMPLE_SIZE = 1500 / DEFAULT_PERCENTILE = 80 ... DEFAULT_OVERHEAD_MIN = 1.0 / ANDROID_OVERHEAD_MIN = 2.0 / MIN_OVERHEAD_MIN = 0.2 / MAX_OVERHEAD_MIN = 4.0".

facts.claim: Retries with the exact same configuration are deliberate because retrying a failing test in isolation often behaves differently; the without-patch phase repeats each failing test 10 times with retry_limit 0 and force_independent_tests, but only when <=100 tests need retrying.

facts.evidence: Chrome ships a new milestone (major version) to the stable channel every two weeks. The new milestone is developed on main for two weeks ... before the milestone's branch is cut, which is then stabilized for three weeks before being shipped to stable.

facts.claim: Once a milestone is on stable it receives weekly 'refreshes' to deploy security fixes and keep the patch gap short.
facts.evidence: Once a milestone reaches stable, weekly updates (called refreshes) are shipped to stable to deploy security fixes and keep Chrome's patch gap short.

facts.claim: Extended Stable now maintains every fourth milestone branch for six additional weeks, shipping a new ES milestone every eight weeks; for its first two weeks stable and ES are identical.

During the first two weeks of this milestone, both stable and extended stable are shipped identical releases

facts.claim: Extended Stable is enterprise-only on Windows and Mac, enabled via policy, and gets weekly refreshes.
facts.evidence: The extended stable channel is only available to enterprises on the Windows and Mac platforms, and can be enabled via enterprise policies. Weekly refreshes are shipped to extended stable.

facts.claim: Security fixes for any platform are landed on the ES branch for embedders, but complex/risky changes (e.g. Site Isolation) may only exist on stable.
facts.evidence: security fixes that are relevant to any Chrome Browser platforms will be landed on the extended stable branch for use by embedders ... complex and risky changes as well as larger features that improve security ... may not be viable to backport

facts.claim: Branch point dates are fixed; release dates can slip and are pre-adjusted around major holidays.
facts.evidence: Branch point dates are fixed, but release dates are subject to change based on a variety of factors (e.g. late-breaking regressions). Release dates are adjusted to avoid shipping new milestones to stable around major holidays

facts.claim: The milestone branch is literally the branch of the daily canary built at branch point.
facts.evidence: The branch generated by the daily canary created at branch point is designated as the milestone branch, which is then stabilized over the following three weeks.

facts.claim: Before branch point: features code-complete, all strings landed, beta blockers addressed; late features punt to the next milestone.
facts.evidence: All new features planned to launch in this milestone should be code complete ... Features which are not code complete by branch point should be punted to the following milestone. All strings should be landed. All beta blocking bugs should be addressed.

facts.claim: Beta promotion happens shortly after branch; the milestone spends two weeks in beta.
facts.evidence: Shortly after branch, the new milestone is shipped to the beta channel for the first time. The milestone spends two weeks total in the beta channel while undergoing stabilization.

facts.claim: Early Stable cut generates a release-candidate shipped to a small percentage of stable users; all stable blockers must be fixed by then.
facts.evidence: Early Stable cut is the day that our early stable release candidate build will be generated. This build is then shipped to a small percentage of stable channel users to gather user feedback. All stable blocking issues must be fixed by early stable cut.

facts.claim: Stable promotion is three weeks after branch point, staged, reaching all users in one to two weeks.

facts.claim: Each stable rollout ships two identical builds differing only in build (patch) number, for A/B statistics; users on the lower number are auto-updated to the higher.

The 24-hour Swarming StateQuery buckets are not a partition: QUERY_DEDUPED tasks are also COMPLETED, QUERY_COMPLETED = QUERY_COMPLETED_SUCCESS + QUERY_COMPLETED_FAILURE, and KILLED/CANCELED overlap, so the sub-counts sum to more than QUERY_ALL (2,627,722 vs 2,417,399 for chromium.tests).
